what_its_for: Vinorelbine is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat non-small cell lung cancer. It works by stopping cancer cells from growing and dividing. Your doctor may also use it for other types of cancer not listed here.
how_to_take: Vinorelbine is usually given as an injection into your vein (IV) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting. It is NOT a pill you take at home. Each infusion usually takes about 6 to 10 minutes. Always follow your care team's exact schedule. Do not try to give yourself this medicine at home.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body size (height and weight). A common starting dose is 25 to 30 mg per square meter of body surface area, given once a week. Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how your body responds and your blood test results. Never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare professional in a clinic, missing a dose means missing your scheduled appointment. If you need to reschedule or miss an appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away. Do not try to 'make up' a missed treatment without talking to your doctor first.
storage: Vinorelbine is stored and handled by healthcare professionals at the clinic. You do not need to store it at home. If you are prescribed an oral form in certain countries, keep it in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C), in the original packaging, and out of reach of children. Do not freeze it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections because this medicine lowers your immune system. Avoid live vaccines (such as flu nasal spray, shingles vaccine, or MMR) while on treatment without asking your doctor first. Avoid becoming pregnant or fathering a child during treatment, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice if taking an oral form. Tell your doctor before taking any new medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (this could be a sign of serious infection), chills or signs of infection, severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that does not stop, numbness, tingling, or weakness in your hands or feet, chest pain or trouble breathing, severe constipation or stomach pain, unusual bruising or bleeding, sores in your mouth that make it hard to eat or drink, signs of a blood clot such as pain or swelling in your leg, or if the IV site becomes red, swollen, or painful after your infusion.
when_it_works: Chemotherapy works over time. It may take several treatment cycles before your doctor can tell how well the medicine is working. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests and imaging scans. It is important to keep all your scheduled appointments even if you feel okay.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and older): May be more sensitive to side effects, especially infection-related complications. Careful monitoring is needed. Pregnancy: Do NOT use during pregnancy. This medicine can seriously harm or cause death to an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after. Men should use contraception during treatment and for 3 months after. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while receiving this medicine. Liver problems: Your dose may need to be lowered if you have liver disease. Your doctor will check your liver function before and during treatment. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established; this medicine is generally not used in children.
